title: Molecular Characterization and Genetic Relatedness of Potential Enteric Pathogens Isolated From Household Drinking Water and Diarrheal Stools of HIV‐Infected Individuals: Implications for Environmental Exposure
content:
Container-stored drinking water in rural South Africa represents a critical potential environmental exposure pathway for enteric bacteria (Escherichia coli, Salmonella, Shigella, and Vibrio spp.) among immunocompromised HIV-infected individuals, underscoring the urgent need for targeted household point-of-use water treatment.


ABSTRACT

The quality of drinking water is critical for immunocompromised populations. This study investigated the prevalence and genetic relatedness of potential enteric bacteria in household container-stored drinking water and diarrheal stools from 164 participants (120 HIV-infected, 44 HIV-negative) in Ugu District, South Africa. In stool specimens, pathogen prevalence was markedly higher among HIV-infected individuals for Escherichia coli (88%), Salmonella spp. (33%), Shigella spp. (27%), and Vibrio spp. (12%) compared to HIV-negative controls (E. coli 34%, Salmonella spp. 2%). Container-stored drinking water in Boboyi showed pathogen detection frequencies exceeding 80%. Molecular analysis of 143 representative isolates (80 water, 63 stool) revealed close genetic clustering between water-derived and clinical E. coli. While these findings highlight significant environmental exposure, conserved 16S rRNA sequences identify container-stored water as a potential exposure source rather than a proven direct transmission vector, underscoring the need for improved household water safety.
